annotations.description: The player chose to be on the draw instead of the play. In Magic: The Gathering, being on the play is almost always advantageous in constructed formats — you get to play lands and develop your board first, apply pressure earlier, and have tempo advantage. The reasoning stated ('play-draw advantage') is backwards: choosing the opponent to go first means YOU are on the draw, not the play. Being on the draw only gives you an extra card, which is generally less valuable than the tempo of going first in constructed.
annotations.actionTaken: Chose the opponent (MiniMx Rules) to take the first turn, putting themselves on the draw.
annotations.betterLine: Choose yourself (Qwen3L Teach) to go first to have the play advantage, which is the default correct choice in nearly all constructed formats.

annotations.description: Bottoming Green Sun's Zenith on a mulligan to 6 is debatable. GSZ is one of the most powerful and flexible cards in the hand - it can tutor for any green creature at any point in the curve and shuffles back into the library. The hand already has three 2-mana green spells (Badgermole Cub, Dredger's Insight, Malevolent Rumble) which are somewhat redundant in the early game. Spymaster's Vault is the weakest land since it enters tapped (no Swamp in play turn 1) and only produces black mana, which none of the current spells need.
annotations.actionTaken: Bottomed Green Sun's Zenith, keeping Badgermole Cub, Dredger's Insight, Malevolent Rumble, Overgrown Tomb, Spymaster's Vault, Verdant Catacombs
annotations.betterLine: Bottom Spymaster's Vault instead. The hand has 3 lands without it (Overgrown Tomb, Verdant Catacombs, plus Catacombs can fetch another), which is sufficient. Keeping GSZ provides a powerful late-game tutor that scales with available mana and can find exactly what's needed. Spymaster's Vault's activated ability requires creatures dying and the hand has no black spells to leverage it.

annotations.description: Playing Watery Grave instead of Bloodstained Mire is slightly suboptimal. Bloodstained Mire should be played first because: (1) It can fetch an untapped Swamp (like Overgrown Tomb or Watery Grave from the deck) without paying the 2 life shock cost if a Swamp is already in play, but more importantly, (2) Playing the fetch land first preserves flexibility - you can crack it later when you know what color you need, and it enables Revolt for Fatal Push. (3) The opponent has a creature (likely Badgermole Cub next turn), and having Revolt available from cracking a fetch land makes Fatal Push significantly better, able to kill creatures with mana value 4 or less instead of just 2 or less. Playing Watery Grave now means next turn you play Bloodstained Mire and can crack it for Revolt, but you could also just play the Mire now, hold it uncracked, and play Watery Grave next turn for the same mana. The key issue is that playing Bloodstained Mire first gives you the option to crack it on the opponent's turn for instant-speed Revolt + Fatal Push if needed, while Watery Grave doesn't provide that flexibility.
annotations.actionTaken: Played Watery Grave as their first land drop
annotations.betterLine: Play Bloodstained Mire first to preserve fetch-crack flexibility for Revolt-enabled Fatal Push on the opponent's turn, then play Watery Grave next turn for Emperor of Bones mana

Both lines produce 2 mana this turn, but Spymaster's Vault preserves fetchland flexibility at no life cost.

With Swamp, the player has 3 black sources and only 1 green, making it harder to cast multiple green spells or use Overgrown Tomb for black toward Yawgmoth while also casting green spells.

annotations.description: Earthbending the Swamp instead of Overgrown Tomb means the animated land only taps for B (one color), whereas Overgrown Tomb taps for B or G. More importantly, the Swamp was just fetched and is a basic — losing it to removal means losing a basic land, while Overgrown Tomb can be recovered the same way (earthbend returns the land tapped when it dies). Additionally, Badgermole Cub's ability adds G when you tap a creature for mana, so animating Overgrown Tomb gives you a creature that can tap for G (getting an additional G from the Cub's triggered ability), providing more mana flexibility. The Swamp as a creature only taps for B with no additional G. With Yawgmoth (BBBB) and green spells in hand, having the dual land as the animated creature that can tap for either color while the basic Swamp stays as a regular land provides better mana development.
annotations.actionTaken: Chose Swamp as the earthbend target for Badgermole Cub's ETB ability.
annotations.betterLine: Choose Overgrown Tomb as the earthbend target, preserving the basic Swamp as a reliable untapped land and getting a more flexible animated creature that taps for B or G (with bonus G from Badgermole Cub).

annotations.description: The player cast Fatal Push in response to the Badgermole Cub's earthbend trigger targeting the opponent's Swamp. The earthbend trigger is already on the stack and will resolve regardless of whether the Cub is alive - killing the source doesn't counter the ability. More importantly, the Fatal Push was cast prematurely. The reasoning even says 'The optimal play is to wait' but then they cast it anyway. By waiting, they could have used Fatal Push during combat to avoid taking damage, or held it to see if a better target appeared. Additionally, the Swamp that was earthbended will become a 1/1 creature with haste - the player could have waited and used Fatal Push on the animated land instead (which would effectively destroy a land since earthbend returns it tapped when it dies). Casting Fatal Push now also means they tapped their only mana source (Watery Grave), leaving them unable to respond to anything else this turn. They also didn't play their Bloodstained Mire before casting the spell, missing a potential revolt trigger opportunity for later.
annotations.actionTaken: Cast Fatal Push targeting Badgermole Cub in response to its earthbend trigger, tapping their only land.
annotations.betterLine: Play Bloodstained Mire first (free land drop), then wait. Could use Fatal Push targeting the animated Swamp land-creature after earthbend resolves (destroying a land is much higher value than killing a 2/2), or hold Fatal Push for combat/later turns to preserve options.

annotations.description: Emperor of Bones has no creature cards exiled with it (the beginning-of-combat exile trigger likely hasn't exiled anything useful yet, or there are no valid targets in graveyards that were exiled by it). Activating Adapt 2 for {1}{B} costs 2 mana and triggers the 'put a creature card exiled with Emperor of Bones onto the battlefield' ability, but if no creature card has been exiled with Emperor of Bones, this trigger does nothing. The player spent 2 mana (their entire available mana this turn) on Adapt 2 with no creature to reanimate, when they could have cast Unearth targeting a creature in the opponent's graveyard (Badgermole Cub) or used Fatal Push defensively. Additionally, Blood Crypt entered tapped so they can't cast Faithless Looting this turn anyway, but wasting mana on a largely empty Adapt trigger is suboptimal.

annotations.description: The player chose not to block the 4/4 Emperor of Bones, taking 4 damage (going from 17 to 13 life). They had a 1/1 animated Swamp (with +1/+1 counter) that could have blocked. The Swamp would die but return to the battlefield tapped as a land due to earthbend's rules. This would be essentially a free chump block - the land comes back, and 4 life is preserved. The player's reasoning even mentions the Swamp but then doesn't use it. Additionally, blocking with the Eldrazi Spawn token (0/1) would also have been acceptable as a chump block to save 4 life, though losing the token means losing the {C} mana source. The animated Swamp block is strictly better since it returns as a land when it dies.

The sequencing seems acceptable, though casting both Walking Ballista (X=1 for 2 mana) and Young Wolf (1 mana) would leave them with more board presence. With 5 mana available, they could cast both - Walking Ballista X=1 (2 mana) + Young Wolf (1 mana) = 3 mana, leaving 2 open. This seems like a missed opportunity to deploy both creatures.

annotations.description: Psychic Frog is a 1/2 blocking Yawgmoth, a 2/4. Psychic Frog deals 1 damage to Yawgmoth (doesn't kill it) and takes 2 damage, dying in the process. The Frog doesn't 'remove' Yawgmoth at all — it just trades itself for 2 damage prevention. Blocking Yawgmoth with the Frog sacrifices the Frog for merely 2 damage prevention (taking 1 from Young Wolf instead of 3 total). The player's reasoning that 'Psychic Frog will survive' is completely wrong — a 1/2 does not survive combat with a 2/4. Additionally, the opponent has Yawgmoth which can sacrifice creatures and draw cards, and killing their own Psychic Frog in combat gives the opponent nothing, but losing this card advantage engine is costly. A better option would have been to not block at all (take 3 damage, going from 15 to 12), or use Fatal Push on Yawgmoth (the more threatening creature) while blocking Young Wolf with Psychic Frog (surviving that block as a 1/2 vs 1/1). Actually, Fatal Push on Yawgmoth requires revolt for mana value 4, and no permanent left the battlefield this turn under Qwen3L's control yet — but Polluted Delta could be cracked to enable revolt, then Fatal Push kills Yawgmoth.
